youtube.title: Python Generator Expressions Explained | Python Programming EP 75
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a generator expression, use it with sum, any and all and tell round brackets from square brackets, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Brackets decide · 0:58 Round brackets · 1:38 List versus generator · 2:12 Second program · 3:12 Recap · 3:42 Bug of the Day · 4:30 Challenge · 4:50 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: A list comprehension builds everything at once. Swap the square brackets for round ones, and it becomes lazy.

scenes.onScreen: "Brackets decide": three numbered lines (1. [x for ...] builds a whole list; 2. (x for ...) makes values on demand; 3. sum, any, all, max accept generators) and an analogy card: a list comprehension with its coat swapped: same recipe, but cooked one dish at a time
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A generator expression looks like a list comprehension, but with round brackets. Instead of building the whole list, it makes values one at a time, as they are needed. Functions that read a sequence once, such as sum, max, any and all, work perfectly with it. When it is the only argument, you can even drop the extra brackets. Think of a list comprehension with its coat swapped. Same recipe, but cooked one dish at a time.

lines: sum, any, all, max accept generators

analogy.title: Think of it like this
analogy.body: a list comprehension with its coat swapped: same recipe, but cooked one dish at a time

scenes.onScreen: genexpr.py: the same recipe, list versus generator
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A list of five numbers. [HL 2] Square brackets build the whole list at once. [HL 3] Round brackets build nothing yet. We get a generator. [HL 4] The list prints one, four, nine, sixteen, twenty five. [HL 5] Sum pulls values from the generator, one at a time. Fifty five. [HL 6] As the only argument, we can drop the extra brackets. Only the odd numbers, squared and added. Thirty five. [HL 7] The longest word length. Five.

code.source:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squares_list = [n * n for n in nums]
squares_gen = (n * n for n in nums)
print(squares_list)
print(sum(squares_gen))
print(sum(n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1))
print(max(len(w) for w in ["sun", "beach", "sea"]))

scenes.onScreen: A full shelf of boxes next to a single box passing along a belt
scenes.animation: A shelf of five filled boxes beside a belt where one box is made at a time and passed to a sum meter
scenes.narration: Here is the difference. A list comprehension fills a whole shelf with finished results, and holds them all in memory. A generator expression keeps a single box on a belt, and makes the next result only when you ask. For small data, either works. For a big or endless source, the generator saves memory, and can start working at once.

objects.text: (n * n ...) one box at a time

scenes.onScreen: anyall.py: any and all stop as soon as the answer is known
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] Four words. [HL 2] Any asks, does at least one word start with c? Crab does. True, and it stops looking there. [HL 3] All asks, is every word longer than three? Sun is not. False, and it stops at once. [HL 4] Next with a generator finds the first match, and gives None if there is none. [HL 5] The first word of length five. Beach. [HL 6] Sum adds the lengths. [HL 7] Fifteen.

code.source:
words = ["sun", "beach", "sea", "crab"]
print(any(w.startswith("c") for w in words))
print(all(len(w) > 3 for w in words))
first = next((w for w in words if len(w) == 5), None)
print(first)
total = sum(len(w) for w in words)
print(total)

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as anyall dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, anyall dot py. The list of squares, then 55, 35, 5. Then True, False, beach, 15.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: Round brackets make a generator expression. Two: It produces values one at a time, on demand. Three: sum, max, any and all accept it directly. Four: Square brackets build the whole list at once. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: printing the generator object
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We print the generator, and see generator object genexpr at a memory address. It holds the recipe, not the values. To see the values, ask for them. Wrap it in list, or loop over it. Remember, doing that uses it up.

props.wrongCode:
squares = (n * n for n in range(4))
print(squares)
props.fixedCode:
squares = (n * n for n in range(4))
print(list(squares))
props.why: A generator holds a recipe, not the values. To see them, loop over it, or pass it to list, sum, or another function that reads it.

shorts.title: Round brackets
shorts.hook: "Take a list comprehension, and swap the square brackets for round ones."
shorts.script: Take a list comprehension, and swap the square brackets for round ones. You get a generator expression. It builds nothing up front. It makes each value only when something asks for it. Same recipe, cooked one dish at a time. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Round brackets are lazy.

shorts.title: Sum a generator
shorts.hook: "Sum, max, min, any and all can read a generator directly."
shorts.script: Sum, max, min, any and all can read a generator directly. Write sum of n times n for n in nums. When it is the only argument, you can skip the extra brackets. No list is ever built in memory. Pause the video and type it out yourself. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.onScreen: sum(n * n for n in nums)
shorts.caption: No list needed.

shorts.title: any and all
shorts.hook: "Any is True as soon as one item matches."
shorts.script: Any is True as soon as one item matches. All is False as soon as one item fails. With a generator, they stop looking right there. For a million words, that saves much time. Say it out loud once. Then you remember it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Stop as soon as you know.

shorts.title: Printing a generator
shorts.hook: "Print a generator, and you see generator object genexpr at an address."
shorts.script: Print a generator, and you see generator object genexpr at an address. That is not a bug in Python. A generator holds a recipe, not the values. Wrap it in list to see the values, or loop over it. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Try it in your own file and watch what happens. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Use list to see values.
